YES!!! Congratulations! 🎉

Eight months of applications, waiting, uncertainty, and pushing forward—and you finally got the job! That is a massive milestone, and you deserve to celebrate it.

I hope you take some time to really enjoy this moment. No more applications hanging over your head, no more refreshing your inbox hoping for good news. You finally get to move on to an exciting new chapter.

How are you feeling? Excited, relieved, still in disbelief, or all three? And tell me about the job! 🥳

s02.html:
Congratulations! Eight months of applications, waiting, and uncertainty is a lot to get through. You finally got the job, and that’s a huge milestone.

You don’t owe the occasion a big celebration tonight. Get something nice to eat, put on something comfortable, and enjoy knowing that the search is finally over. Relief can be its own kind of celebration.

The excitement can come later, when you’ve had some proper rest. I’m really happy for you.

s03.html:
Not yet. Based on this opening line alone, I would recommend revising before submitting to literary agents.

There are three main weaknesses:

  • “It was a dark and stormy night” is a well-known literary cliché. Unless you're deliberately using it for parody or subverting readers' expectations, it risks making your opening feel unoriginal.
  • “Sarah was sad” tells rather than evokes emotion. Readers know what Sarah is feeling, but they have no reason to share that feeling or become invested in her.
  • “Very very sad” lacks emotional precision. Is Sarah grieving, heartbroken, lonely, disappointed, or devastated? Each suggests a different character and story.

The underlying concept—a woman experiencing emotional distress during a storm—is perfectly workable. The execution just needs more specificity, atmosphere, and narrative intrigue.

For example, depending on your intended tone:

Literary fiction:

Sarah had spent the evening listening to the rain, grateful for anything loud enough to drown out her thoughts.

Mystery:

By midnight, the rain had washed away every trace of him except the photograph Sarah couldn't bring herself to burn.

Contemporary fiction:

Sarah had promised herself she wouldn't cry again, but apparently even that was a promise she couldn't keep.

Dark comedy:

The weather was miserable, Sarah was miserable, and the only thing enjoying the evening was the leak in her bedroom ceiling.

These aren't necessarily the right openings for your novel, but they demonstrate how specificity and narrative voice can transform a simple premise.

A strong opening doesn't have to be spectacular, poetic, or dramatic. It does, however, need to give the reader a reason to continue.

I'd challenge you to rewrite the line without using the words dark, stormy, sad, or very. Think about what Sarah is doing, what has happened to her, and what makes this particular night worth beginning a novel with.

One weak opening sentence doesn't mean you have a weak novel. But in a competitive querying environment, you want your first page to demonstrate the quality and distinctiveness of your writing as quickly as possible. This line isn't doing that yet.

Funny how a sound you never chose can become part of what home feels like. The radiator clunking, the heat coming on, the quiet reassurance that everything was doing what it always did.

There’s something particularly bittersweet about realizing you’ve heard an ordinary sound for the last time. You probably never thought to listen to it properly, until today.

s12.html:
Sometimes it’s the smallest thing that makes a difficult week feel unbearable. The leaking sink and the rent were already weighing on you, and then even making a simple meal went wrong. I can understand why the rice was what got to you.

Since Mr. Okonkwo has been decent so far, I’d keep the message respectful, straightforward, and sincere without overexplaining or apologizing excessively.

You could send him this tomorrow:

Good morning, Mr. Okonkwo. I wanted to let you know in advance that my rent payment will be delayed this month due to some financial difficulties. I apologize for the inconvenience and expect to be able to make the payment by [date]. I appreciate your patience and understanding, and I wanted to keep you informed rather than leave you waiting.

If you're unsure when you'll be able to pay, don't commit to a date you might not be able to meet. Instead, say that you'll update him by a specific day.

As for tonight, you don't have to solve everything at once. The landlord's message is drafted. The sink can be dealt with separately. If you haven't eaten, get yourself something simple, even if it isn't much of a dinner.

And you're allowed to be upset about the rice. It may have been a small thing, but it happened at the end of a long week when you probably just wanted one thing to go right.

s15.html:
Of course. I’m happy to keep you company for a while.

Friday nights can feel especially lonely when everyone else seems to have something going on. There's something about the expectation that you're supposed to be out having fun that makes an otherwise quiet evening feel a little emptier.

We don't have to talk about anything particularly important, though. We can chat about random things, trade unpopular opinions, play a little game, talk about life, or just have one of those conversations that wanders from one topic to another.

So, what does your Friday night look like right now? Are you curled up on the couch, lying in bed scrolling through your phone, having a drink, or just sitting around wondering what to do?

And what's the mood tonight—bored, lonely, restless, or just wishing you had someone to hang out with?

s19.html:
There's something particularly painful about being estranged from someone who has been such a significant part of your life, especially when you're not sure you want that closeness back.

You can miss your sister without wanting to speak to her. You can feel relief at the distance and still grieve what you've lost. You might not even know which of those feelings is stronger right now.

And there's the weight of not knowing whether this is a temporary silence or something more permanent.

We don't have to make sense of it or turn it into a decision. I can sit with you in that uncertainty. You don't have to want reconciliation, and you don't have to want the estrangement to last, either. Whatever you're feeling about her can be complicated and unfinished.

s20.html:
Honesty is a strength, but how you express it can determine whether it strengthens a relationship or damages it.

There’s a difference between being honest and being unnecessarily hurtful. You can tell the truth while still being considerate, tactful, and receptive to someone else's feelings. Being kind doesn't require being dishonest.

Since your last three relationships ended in what you perceive to be a similar way, it might be worth examining a few things:

  • Intent: Were you being honest to build understanding, resolve a problem, or simply express your frustration?
  • Delivery: Did you communicate your thoughts respectfully, or did honesty sometimes come across as criticism or judgment?
  • Timing: Did you consider when and how to raise sensitive subjects?
  • Reciprocity: Were you as comfortable receiving uncomfortable truths as you were expressing them?
  • Compatibility: Were your partners genuinely unwilling to engage in difficult but necessary conversations?

It's entirely possible that your previous partners struggled with honest communication. It's also possible that something about your communication style contributed to the pattern. Both can be true.

You don't need to abandon honesty to have a successful relationship. The goal is to combine honesty with empathy, self-awareness, and emotional maturity.

What’s an example of something you said in one of those relationships that you felt your partner couldn't handle? That would help distinguish between a partner rejecting an uncomfortable truth and a partner reacting to how that truth was communicated.
